newsitem.title: CANADA: Ottawa talks open on launch of Zaire rescue plan.
newsitem.headline: Ottawa talks open on launch of Zaire rescue plan.

text.p: Ambassadors of key nations that have agreed to join a scaled-down mission to help refugees in eastern Zaire began meeting in Ottawa on Friday to give formal approval to the force.

The meeting, which involved about a dozen nations, aimed to give the go-ahead to launch the mission, starting with a military headquarters in Entebbe, Uganda, as well as reconnaissance missions and possible airdrops.

It came nearly three weeks after Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien began urging world leaders to rescue what aid agencies then said were more than a million refugees and displaced people in eastern Zaire.
Since then about 600,000 refugees have returned to Rwanda, but Western officials have identified at least 200,000 more and believe there could be hundreds of thousands of others.

"I'm not saying it's a panacea, (that) it's a full answer," Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy told Parliament, seeking to allay concerns voiced by an opposition member about whether airdrops were the best route. "But I do know that most Canadians ... want this country to continue to provide leadership to mobilize ... the international community to support humanitarian aid."

More than 20 countries, including the United States, France, Belgium, Japan, Senegal and South Africa, have agreed to contribute to the Canadian-led mission. The meeting was to end around 3 p.m. EST (2000 GMT) after which the mission could in theory begin, foreign affairs spokesman John Bell said.

The force would be much smaller than the 10,000 Chretien had originally envisaged. The new size was still not known but Canada already has positioned almost 300 people and the United States almost 400 in the area, mostly in Entebbe. Senegal has offered 800 troops.
On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of Defense William Perry said he was unable to say if more U.S. troops would be committed.

Some aid workers in the area have suggested airdrops would be expensive, dangerous and might get aid into the wrong hands. Zairian Information Minister Boguo Makeli said the Zairian government would not allow overflights to this end.

Axworthy said on Thursday that the preference would be to use ground convoys if possible. But, addressing Parliament on Friday, he said Canada "did consult very clearly with the major humanitarian organizations before we put the proposal forward."
He dismissed Makeli's remark as a "comment by one minister of one of the governments in Zaire ... There's total confusion in Zaire. No one is sure who's in control."

"The fact is that we have received the full approval of the president of Zaire (Mobutu Sese Seko) in the discussions with Ambassador Chretien," he added. Canadian Ambassador Raymond Chretien is the U.N. envoy seeking to bring about a long-term solution to the crisis.

His uncle, Prime Minister Chretien, said during a visit to Japan that Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, commander of the international force, had secured agreement in principle on air drops from the Tutsi rebels that control eastern Zaire.

Axworthy made clear in a statement on Thursday that airdrops would be used only "if needed." He added that further reconnaissance would be the first priority to determine exactly where food was needed.
